searchNote: Second check. WebSearch summaries only (WebFetch could not resolve hosts, so no page was read in full; every "confirmed" below rests on a search summary of encyclopedia, library, publisher, university or catalogue pages plus the checker's own knowledge). ode.js, elegy.js and light-novel.js were all searched in this pass. villanelle.js is unchanged from the first check (already installed).

firstPass.method: own knowledge only (search budget exhausted before this file); lint OK

corrected.was: the stand in a different one (presented as the meaning of epode)
corrected.now: the closing part in a different one, which Ben Jonson called the stand
corrected.why: Epode is Greek for an after-song; turn, counter-turn and stand are Jonson's English names for the three parts.

corrected.where: history, last point: Campos Triumphal Ode
corrected.was: wrote the Triumphal Ode (1915) to machines and cities
corrected.now: published the Triumphal Ode in 1915, a poem of the modern machine age
corrected.why: Written 1914, published in Orpheu in 1915; the subject is the modern industrial age, so the narrower 'machines and cities' was dropped.

corrected.now: the Triumphal Ode (published 1915) by Alvaro de Campos
corrected.why: Same date correction: 1915 is the publication year, not the writing year.

softened.was: The earliest odes were sung by a chorus
softened.now: Many early Greek odes were sung by a chorus
softened.why: Some early Greek lyric (Sappho, Alcaeus) was solo song; choral performance is not true of all of them.

softened.was: in the early seventeenth century ... Cary and Morison (about 1629)
softened.now: in the seventeenth century ... (composed around 1629)
softened.why: The composition date is approximate; the period label was loosened to match.

softened.was: published for the duke's state funeral
softened.now: published at the time of the duke's state funeral
softened.why: Safer wording for a publication that coincided with the funeral.

softened.was: Marvell's Horatian Ode ... follows Horace's balance and tone
softened.now: is named for Horace's balance and restraint
softened.why: Marvell's stanza is not a Horatian metre; the claim is about the name and manner only.

softened.was: qasida ... is commonly translated as ode
softened.now: is often translated as ode
softened.why: Translation practice varies.

softened.was: from about fifty lines to a few hundred
softened.now: from a few dozen lines to a few hundred
softened.why: Keats's To Autumn (33 lines) falls below fifty.

corrected.was: Romantic-era odes turned inward: Schiller's An die Freude (written 1785, ...), then Coleridge, Wordsworth, Keats, Shelley
corrected.now: Late eighteenth-century and Romantic-era odes widened the form: Schiller's An die Freude (written 1785, ...), then Coleridge, Wordsworth, Keats, Shelley
corrected.why: Schiller's poem (written summer 1785, printed 1786 in Thalia, confirmed by search) is a communal hymn to joy from before the Romantic period, so "Romantic-era" and "turned inward" did not describe it. All the dates in the point were confirmed (Coleridge 1802, Wordsworth 1807, Shelley 1820, Beethoven 1824).

softened.was: published at the time of the duke's state funeral
softened.now: published in the week of the duke's state funeral
softened.why: Funeral was 18 November 1852; search sources give the ode's publication as 16, 17 or 18 November and disagree, so only the week is asserted.

softened.was: Odas elementales (1954) praised onions, tomatoes and other plain things
softened.now: Odas elementales (1954) praised the onion and other plain things
softened.why: Britannica ties the onion ode to the 1954 book (year 1954 confirmed); the tomato ode's place in that volume was only supported by weak sources (a translation page and a retailer listing), so it was dropped from the text. The socks ode is in the 1956 second volume and is not mentioned.

softened.was: Marvell's Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland is named for Horace's balance and restraint
softened.now: Marvell's Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland (written 1650) draws on Horace for its poise and restraint
softened.why: Search supports 1650 and a scholarly view that the poem owes much to Horace Odes 1.37; "named for his balance and restraint" over-read the title.

softened.was: Latin for seize the day
softened.now: Latin, usually rendered seize the day
softened.why: Odes 1.11 is confirmed as the source, but the "seize" rendering is a later English convention and "pluck" or "harvest" are also argued.

confirmedBySearch: Horace Odes books 1 to 3 published 23 BCE, book 4 (15 poems) in 13 BCE (the text states only "a fourth some years later"; some scholars dispute joint publication of 1 to 3).
Ronsard's Quatre premiers livres des Odes, 1550 (January 1550; one auction catalogue says 1549), imitating Pindar and Horace.
Jonson's Cary-Morison ode: written shortly after Morison's death in 1629; first printed in the 1640 Workes; sections named Turn, Counter-Turn and Stand (so "which Ben Jonson called the stand" holds).
Cowley's Pindarique Odes within the 1656 folio Poems; Congreve's 1706 Discourse on the Pindarique Ode argues Pindar was regular and Cowley's imitators were not.
Collins's Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegorical Subjects: entered in the printer's ledger 15 Dec 1746, title page dated 1747.
Gray's Progress of Poesy and The Bard in Odes by Mr. Gray, 1757, Strawberry Hill, both strophe/antistrophe/epode (triadic) Pindarics.
Schiller An die Freude written 1785, printed 1786 in Thalia; Beethoven's Ninth completed and performed 1824.

Coleridge Dejection: An Ode drafted 4 April 1802, printed in the Morning Post 4 October 1802; Shelley West Wind written 1819 near Florence, printed 1820 in the Prometheus Unbound volume, five 14-line sections of terza rima tercets and a couplet.
Wordsworth's ode in Poems, in Two Volumes, 1807 (under the title "Ode"), irregular Pindaric in form.
Campos's Ode Triunfal composed 1914, first printed in Orpheu no. 1 (March 1915), a celebration of machines and the modern age.
Gray's cat ode written 22 Feb to 1 Mar 1747, first printed anonymously in Dodsley's Collection of Poems, 1748.
Dryden's Alexander's Feast written for the 1697 St Cecilia's Day festival (22 November 1697).
Keats's Nightingale (8 stanzas), Grecian Urn (5) and Melancholy (3) each use ten-line stanzas.
Shijing alternate English title Book of Odes; qasida "often translated as ode", monorhyme, praise a main use (Britannica).
Pindar's datable victory odes run from 498 BCE to 446 BCE; stasimon is a choral ode between episodes; Greek ode word from aoide, song; carpe diem is from Odes 1.11.
remainingDoubts: Search summaries were the only web source (WebFetch cannot resolve hosts); no page was read in full, and several summaries came from Wikipedia, Britannica and catalogue records rather than editions.
Pindar's works year "c. 470 BCE" is only a midpoint of his datable odes (about 498 to 446 BCE, confirmed), kept to match the library's existing work record.
The publication day of Tennyson's Wellington ode is disputed (16, 17 or 18 November 1852), so the text says only "in the week of" the funeral.

The Neruda tomato ode was not confirmed to be in the 1954 volume by search (recall says it is), so only the onion is named; the profile's other Neruda wording ("everyday foods and objects", "ordinary things") is general and consistent with Britannica.
"Regular Pindarics" for Gray means the triadic strophe/antistrophe/epode shape (confirmed); it is critical convention, not a count of identical metres.
The Princeton Encyclopedia of Poetry and Poetics is cited as a reference by title only; it was not searched for its ode entry.
The line-length range ("a few dozen to a few hundred") is a rough statement checked only against well-known examples (Keats's To Autumn about 33 lines, the Wellington ode a few hundred), not a count.

corrected.was: Rilke's Duino Elegies, which take their name from the mournful mood
corrected.now: named for the castle near Trieste where he began them
corrected.why: The title comes from Duino Castle, not from a mood.

corrected.was: Ben Jonson's poem on his first son (1616)
corrected.now: On My First Sonne (printed 1616 among his epigrams and often read as an elegy)
corrected.why: The poem is titled and printed as an epigram; calling it an elegy outright was misleading.

corrected.now: a term coined by John Ruskin in the nineteenth century
corrected.why: Ruskin coined it in Modern Painters in the 1850s; stated plainly.

corrected.was: from the Greek and Latin for a funeral song
corrected.now: from the Greek epikedeion, a funeral song
corrected.why: The Latin word is a borrowing from the Greek.

softened.was: writing in the late first century BCE
softened.now: writing from the later first century BCE
softened.why: Ovid was active into the first century CE.

softened.was: is an elegy of homesickness
softened.now: gathers poems of exile and homesickness in elegiac couplets
softened.why: More exact description of the work.

softened.was: From the sixteenth century elegy came in English to mean a poem of mourning
softened.now: In English the word came to mean mainly a poem of mourning by the seventeenth century
softened.why: The exact century of the shift was not certain; the later bound is safe.

softened.was: the grief memoir has taken over some of its ground in prose
softened.now: prose grief memoirs now sit beside the elegy as a kindred way of writing about loss
softened.why: The original was an unsupported claim about one form displacing another.

softened.was: Goethe's Roman Elegies (1795)
softened.now: (published 1795)
softened.why: The poems were written 1788 to 1790 and published in 1795.

softened.was: a stanza often called the elegiac stanza
softened.now: often called the elegiac stanza (or heroic quatrain), though earlier poets used it
softened.why: Gray did not invent the stanza; the name is a convention.

softened.was: so called because of that poem
softened.now: often named after that poem and also called the heroic quatrain
softened.why: Same softening.

softened.was: the most quoted English elegy
softened.now: among the best-known English elegies
softened.why: A superlative that cannot be verified.

softened.was: the Greek threnos means a wailing
softened.now: from the Greek threnos, a lament or dirge
softened.why: More defensible gloss.

softened.was: the pastoral poems of Theocritus and of the later Greek poets Bion and Moschus, and Virgil's Eclogues, set the pattern of a shepherd mourning a shepherd
softened.now: Theocritus's song for the herdsman Daphnis, the lament for Bion traditionally credited to Moschus, and Virgil's Eclogues set the pattern of a shepherd mourning a shepherd
softened.why: Search sources say Theocritus Idyll 1 is the source of the pastoral lament, Bion wrote the Lament for Adonis, and the Lament for Bion is traditionally credited to Moschus but probably by a pupil of Bion; Virgil's Fifth Eclogue mourns Daphnis. The new wording names what is documented and keeps the attribution honest.

confirmedBySearch: Tyrtaeus (war), Mimnermus (love, wine), Solon (politics), Theognis as archaic Greek elegists in elegiac couplets (hexameter then pentameter).
Tibullus (died 19 BCE), Propertius (first book about 28 BCE) and Ovid's Amores as Augustan love elegy; "from the later first century BCE" holds.
Exeter Book copied about 975 (Britannica), containing The Wanderer, The Seafarer and The Ruin; "later tenth century" holds.
Spenser's Astrophel printed 1595 in the Colin Clouts volume, a pastoral elegy for Sir Philip Sidney.
Lycidas written 1637, first printed 1638 in Justa Edouardo King Naufrago; Milton's 1645 note calls it a Monody.
Gray's Elegy 1751; abab iambic pentameter quatrains, called the elegiac or heroic stanza.

Arnold's Thyrsis (1866) for Clough; Adonais (1821) for Keats; In Memoriam A.H.H. published 1850 for Arthur Hallam, abba tetrameter stanza; Whitman's lilac elegy first printed 1865 in Sequel to Drum-Taps.
Jonson's On My First Sonne appeared in the 1616 folio among the Epigrams and is read as an elegy.
Hardy's Poems of 1912-13 for Emma, in Satires of Circumstance (November 1914); Auden's In Memory of W. B. Yeats first published 1939 (New Republic, 8 March), collected 1940.
Goethe's Roman Elegies written 1788 to 1790, published 1795 in Die Horen; Donne's love elegies are a recognised group in modern editions.
Rilke's Duino Elegies begun at Duino Castle near Trieste (1912), completed 1922, published 1923.
Ramazani, Poetry of Mourning (1994): modern elegies often do not reach the consolation Sacks's model expects; Sacks, The English Elegy (1985).
Ruskin's pathetic fallacy appears in Modern Painters III (sources give 1854 or 1856, so only "nineteenth century" is asserted).
Urdu marsiya of Mir Anis and Mirza Dabir (nineteenth-century Lucknow, Karbala subject); Caoineadh Airt Uí Laoghaire for Art Ó Laoghaire killed in 1773.
remainingDoubts: Search summaries were the only web source (WebFetch cannot resolve hosts); no page was read in full.
Ovid's exile from 8 CE and the Tristia in elegiac couplets were not covered by the search results and rest on the checker's own knowledge (well established).
The epicedium (Greek epikedeion) and threnody (Greek threnos) etymologies were not covered by search; they are stated loosely and rest on standard dictionary knowledge.
Lycidas is dated 1638 in the works list (first printing) while the library's genre entry lists 1637 (composition); the text gives both.
The Ruskin year is given as 1854 by some sources and 1856 by others, so the text does not name a year.
Auden's poem was first published in March 1939 (New Republic confirmed; a London Mercury appearance was not confirmed); the text asserts only 1939.
The name "elegiac stanza" for Gray's quatrain follows handbook usage (Thomas Gray Archive, Shmoop and enotes agree); handbooks differ and earlier poets used the stanza.
The Art Ó Laoghaire lament is dated by the 1773 killing; authorship and composition history are discussed by scholars, and the text names no author.

villanelle.js.method: web search summaries for most claims; lint OK

corrected.was: W. H. Auden's If I Could Tell You appeared in 1940
corrected.now: W. H. Auden wrote If I Could Tell You in 1940
corrected.why: Written 1940 (dated October 1940 by his editor); first printed in a magazine in early 1941 according to a scholar of the form.

corrected.was: Mid-century: ... If I Could Tell You (1940)
corrected.now: Twentieth century: ... If I Could Tell You (written 1940)
corrected.why: Same date issue; 1940 is not a first-publication year.

corrected.was: Early twentieth century: Robinson's The House on the Hill, from the 1890s
corrected.now: Late nineteenth century: ... written in the 1890s, often cited as an early American villanelle
corrected.why: A poem of the 1890s is not early twentieth century (first version 1894, collected in 1896).

corrected.was: nineteenth-century writers on French verse took Passerat's poem as the pattern ... so most Renaissance villanelles do not match it
corrected.now: French writers on verse after the Renaissance, up to Banville's 1872 handbook, took Passerat's poem as the pattern, and scholars disagree about who first fixed it; most other Renaissance villanelles are looser songs
corrected.why: Sources trace the fixing to eighteenth-century dictionary makers, to Tenint in 1844, or to Banville; they disagree.

corrected.was: after Edmund Gosse's 1877 essay ... belongs to the same moment
corrected.now: late 1870s and 1880s, helped by Gosse's 1877 essay ... Wilde's Theocritus (1881) belongs to the same fashion
corrected.why: Dobson's villanelle appeared in 1877 itself, so 'after' the essay was too strict; Wilde's poem is in his 1881 Poems.

corrected.was: mid-twentieth-century poems by Auden, Thomas, Roethke, Plath and Bishop
corrected.why: Bishop's One Art is 1976, not mid-century.

softened.was: became the best-known villanelle in English
softened.now: is widely regarded as the best-known villanelle in English
softened.why: A superlative stated as opinion.

softened.was: many villanelles speak to a lover or the dead
softened.now: some villanelles ...
softened.why: No count supports 'many'.

softened.was: between the late 1940s and 1953
softened.now: between the late 1940s and the early 1950s
softened.why: Plath's villanelle was written about 1951 and printed in 1953; Roethke's appeared in his 1953 book.

removed.where: canon works list: If I Could Tell You, W. H. Auden, 1940
removed.why: Year is not the first-publication year (written 1940, reported first printed 1941 in a magazine, collected 1945) and could not be fixed from two sources. The poem stays in the text as 'written 1940'. Canon keeps 5 works.

remainingDoubts: Passerat's J'ay perdu ma tourterelle: printed in the 1606 Recueil (confirmed by search, after his death in 1602); one source gives composition as 1574. Passerat's dates 1534 to 1602 were confirmed by search.
Auden's first publication was reported in a single scholarly web source as a magazine in early 1941; not confirmed by a second source, which is why the work record was removed.

W. E. Henley's A Dainty Thing's the Villanelle: poem exists and is about the form; its year (about 1877 in London magazine, 1888 in A Book of Verses) was not confirmed, so the text only says Henley wrote early examples in the 1870s and 1880s.
Roethke's The Waking: first appearance found only in the 1953 book; an earlier magazine appearance was not ruled out.
Robinson's House on the Hill is described as 'often cited as an early American villanelle'; no source calls it the first.
The terzanelle is credited to Lewis Turco (search summaries agree); its date and exact scheme are not stated and handbooks differ.
Rondeau, pantoum, sestina and ghazal descriptions in the compare facet are standard textbook definitions, not re-checked by search.

light-novel.js.method: second check with WebSearch summaries (first checker's search budget ran out part-way); lint OK

corrected.was: Dengeki Bunko hits that came through its new-author prize: Boogiepop and Others (1998) and Kino's Journey (2000)
corrected.now: Dengeki Bunko hits from writers its new-author prize brought in: ...
corrected.why: Boogiepop and Others won the fourth Dengeki (Game) Novel Prize (1997) and was published in February 1998, but Sigsawa's Kino's Journey was a finalist for the sixth prize and then serialised (March 2000) with the first book on 10 July 2000, so "came through the prize" overstated it for Kino.

corrected.was: Years here usually mean the first volume in print, except where the conv text notes an earlier web posting
corrected.now: Years here usually mean the first volume in print; Re:Zero's year is its web start (printed 2014)
corrected.why: The note contradicted the works list: Sword Art Online is listed by its 2009 print year although its conv point also mentions web posting, while Re:Zero is listed by its 2012 web start (the library's other records use 2012). The note now says what the list actually does.

softened.was: Romance, historical romance and light literary lines: some imprints aim at young women or at older readers, sometimes called light literature, with illustrated covers but quieter, more adult subject matter
softened.now: Romance and light literary lines: some imprints aim at older or adult readers with quieter, more everyday stories, a shelf sometimes called light literature (raito bungei) in Japan, and its border with the light novel is blurry
softened.why: Search confirms raito bungei as a Japanese category between light novels and general fiction with a blurry border and quieter, more realistic stories; it did not confirm "young women", "historical romance" or "illustrated covers" (sources suggest fewer illustrations), so those were dropped.

confirmedBySearch: Vampire Hunter D by Hideyuki Kikuchi, first novel 1983, called a forerunner.
Fujimi Fantasia Bunko established 1988; Slayers entered the first Fantasia Awards 1989, began in Dragon Magazine in 1989 and was published as a Fantasia Bunko novel in 1990.
Light novel as a term: credited to Kamikita Keita, sysop of the SF and Fantasy forum on Nifty-Serve, around 1990 (the exact year is loose in sources); early 1994 newspaper use cited.

Dengeki Bunko established June 1993 (first book Crystania); Boogiepop and Others, Dengeki Game Novel Prize 1997, published 25 February 1998; Boogiepop widely credited with launching the category's popularity.
Kino's Journey first volume 10 July 2000 under Dengeki Bunko.
Haruhi Suzumiya: first novel June 2003 (Sneaker Bunko); anime aired April to July 2006; English edition by Little, Brown with Yen Press from April 2009.
Kono Light Novel ga Sugoi first edition released 26 November 2004 (the 2005 listing), by Takarajimasha.
Sword Art Online: written 2001, not submitted to the Dengeki Game Novel Prize because it ran over the page limit, posted online from 2002, printed by Dengeki Bunko April 2009.
Shosetsuka ni Naro opened 2 April 2004; Re:Zero web serial from April 2012, first volume in print January 2014 (MF Bunko J).
Spice and Wolf volume 1 listed as 10 February 2006 (Dengeki Bunko, Dengeki Novel Prize silver 2005); Toradora! volume 1 on 10 March 2006.
Bunkobon is A6 (10.5 by 14.8 cm); a light novel averages about 50,000 words; colour pages at the front, black-and-white pictures inside.
English light novels were few in the 2000s (Slayers by Tokyopop from 2004, Seven Seas from 2007, Haruhi from 2009) and grew around 2013.

Kuchi-e is the Japanese word for a frontispiece; komikaraizu is the loanword for turning a novel or other work into manga; media mix means one work spread across novel, manga, anime and games; label (reberu) is the term used for light novel imprints such as Dengeki Bunko and Fujimi Fantasia Bunko.
remainingDoubts: Search summaries were the only web source (WebFetch cannot resolve hosts); no page was read in full, and many came from Wikipedia and fan or retail pages rather than publisher records.
Atogaki (afterword) and shinjin-sho (new-author prize) are standard Japanese words checked from the checker's own knowledge; the search returned no page that defines them for light novels.

Spice and Wolf: one search summary (a fan encyclopedia) gives June 2006 for the series start against 10 February 2006 in Wikipedia's volume list; the text asserts only the year 2006, which holds either way.
Re:Zero is listed as 2012 (web start, matching the library's other records); the text says printed in 2014.
The Nifty-Serve origin of the term "light novel" rests on one source naming Kamikita Keita and "around 1990"; the text says "usually traced" and "around 1990".
Raito bungei was confirmed only as an existing, blurry category; its imprints and readership were not confirmed, which is why the claims about them were removed.
The word-count range (forty to sixty thousand) agrees with the library's light-novel entry and with a source giving about fifty thousand on average, but practice differs by imprint and prize.
